description:
We are a passionate team of creators, developers, and tech enthusiasts hailing from the heart of Romania, right where the legendary Carpathian Mountains meet the infinite cosmos.

We are fascinated by space exploration, data analysis, coding, and turning creative ideas into real-world technological solutions. We combine local grit and innovation with a shared dream of exploring the universe.
summary: Outpost 30 is a browser game where a student commands four astronauts on the Moon or Mars for 30 days. Each day the player reads a power forecast and splits a limited supply of kilowatts between life support, a greenhouse, a radiation shield and a science lab. Dust storms, dark periods, solar storms and equipment failures force real trade-offs, and a debrief at the end explains why the mission succeeded or failed. It addresses the challenge by keeping one authentic engineering trade-off at the centre of a ten-minute game that 9 to 14 year olds can play on any phone or laptop, using published NASA figures for oxygen, water recycling and radiation.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The player picks a landing site (Shackleton Rim on the Moon or Jezero Crater on Mars) and a rank (Cadet with daily hints, or Commander). Each day they see the outpost, six gauges (oxygen, water, food, battery, radiation, crew health), a five-day power forecast, and four systems that all want the same power: life support, greenhouse, shield rover and science lab. They set the levels and run the day. A plain-language log explains every change.

HOW IT TEACHES TRADE-OFFS

Nothing is free. Science is the purpose of the mission, but the lab needs power and crew time. Shielding has to be built before a solar storm, at the cost of science now. A greenhouse takes days to pay back. Repairs close the lab. The two sites fail in different ways: the Moon punishes late shielding, Mars punishes an empty battery during a dust storm.

WHY IT HOLDS ATTENTION

One decision per day, about a minute per day, a drawn outpost that changes with the player's choices, and events that carry a true story ("It really happened"), such as the 1972 solar storm between Apollo 16 and 17 or the dust storm that ended the Opportunity mission. The debrief gives a mission patch, charts of every resource, what a real mission planner would say, and discussion questions.

INTENDED IMPACT

A teacher can run it in one lesson. A 4-digit mission code reproduces the same storms and events, so a whole class can play the same mission and compare decisions. It needs no install, no account and collects no data, so it works on school tablets and family phones.

TOOLS

One HTML file with plain JavaScript, CSS and inline SVG. No framework and no backend. A seeded random generator makes missions reproducible. A test script plays 2,400 missions with three scripted strategies to check the balance: careless play loses, careful play survives, and the gold patch needs skill.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We used published figures (0.84 kg of oxygen per astronaut per day, 98% water recovery, 0.67 mSv per day on Mars, 1.37 mSv per day on the Moon) and listed every simplification in the README: power comes in whole blocks, the greenhouse is more productive than a real one, and solar storm doses are tuned so shielding matters within 30 days.

NEXT STEPS

Romanian and Spanish translations, optional live space-weather missions from NASA DONKI, a 500-day Mars mission, and a teacher guide.

The code, design and text were generated with an AI assistant (Claude), directed and reviewed by the team.
